glossary.definition: A small chunk of text, like a syllable or short word, that the AI reads as one unit instead of reading letter by letter.
A program that splits your text into tokens before sending it to the AI model.
A free tool from OpenAI that counts exactly how many tokens your text uses, without making any API call.

hook.scenario: You paste a 1,000-word essay into GPT-4o. The context limit is 128,000 tokens. Before you hit Send, predict: will this essay use around 1,000 tokens, more, or fewer?
hook.question: Make your prediction, then read on to see if you are right — and why 'token' is not the same as 'word'.

mental_model.intuition: A token is a chunk of text — roughly a word, a syllable, or a punctuation mark — that the model reads as one unit.
mental_model.description: LLMs never read characters or whole words. They read tokens. A tokenizer splits your text into tokens before the model sees it. Common English words are usually one token each. Rare words, code, and non-English text split into several tokens. On average, 1 token = about 4 characters in English. Every price, context limit, and rate limit on the OpenAI pricing page is in tokens, not words.

illustration.alt: The phrase 'unbelievable pricing' split into four sub-word token tiles, counted as 4 tokens.

sections.body: When you call the API, a tokenizer runs first. It turns your raw text into a list of integer IDs. Each ID maps to one sub-word piece. The model never sees letters — it sees these IDs. When the model replies, a de-tokenizer turns the IDs back into text.
sections.recap: Text → token IDs → model → token IDs → text. The model never touches raw letters.

sections.body: Why sub-words, not whole words? A whole-word list would need millions of entries for all words, plurals, and proper nouns. Sub-word tokenizers (OpenAI uses one called BPE) work with a fixed vocabulary of about 100,000 pieces. Unknown words split into known pieces. For example: 'unbelievable' → ['un', 'believ', 'able']. This handles all languages without an infinite dictionary.
sections.recap: BPE sub-word tokenization: fixed vocabulary, unknown words split into known pieces.

sections.body: Token count controls three things: cost (you pay per token in and out), speed (more tokens = more time), and context limits (the model has a hard cap on total tokens per call — input plus output combined). The 128k context window on `gpt-4o` means 128,000 tokens, not words. In English, 1,000 tokens is roughly 750 words.
sections.recap: Tokens are the billing and limits unit. 1,000 English tokens ≈ 750 words.

sections.body: You can count tokens before making any API call. The `tiktoken` library mirrors OpenAI's tokenizer exactly. It runs on your computer and costs nothing. Use it to check your token count before you send, so you never hit the context limit by surprise.
sections.recap: Use `tiktoken` locally to count tokens before calling the API — free and instant.

sections.body: **Non-English text and code use more tokens per word than English prose.** A Chinese character may be 1–2 tokens. A rare technical term in English can be 3–4 tokens. The same content can cost very differently depending on language and domain. Teams who budget by word count often get a surprise when they switch languages.
sections.recap: Tokens, not words, control cost and limits — and they vary a lot by language and domain.

code_snippets.title: Count tokens before making an API call
code_snippets.code:
import tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model('gpt-4o')
text = 'unbelievable pricing for the new plan'
tokens = enc.encode(text)

print(len(tokens))        # 7
print(enc.decode(tokens)) # same text back
code_snippets.explanation: `tiktoken` mirrors OpenAI's tokenizer exactly and makes no network call. Use this to count tokens before you send, to prevent silent context-overflow errors and to budget before you pay.

code_snippets.title: Count tokens in a messages[] list — the real billing unit
code_snippets.code:
import tiktoken

def count_messages_tokens(messages: list[dict], model='gpt-4o') -> int:
    enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model(model)
    total = 0
    for msg in messages:
        # 4 tokens overhead per message (role + delimiters)
        total += 4 + len(enc.encode(msg.get('content', '')))
    total += 2  # reply priming tokens
    return total

msgs = [
    {'role': 'system', 'content': 'You are a helpful assistant.'},
    {'role': 'user',   'content': 'Explain RAG in one sentence.'},
]
print(count_messages_tokens(msgs))  # ~27
code_snippets.explanation: The API bills the full `messages[]` array, not just the user message. Each message carries about 4 overhead tokens for its role tags. In a long conversation, this adds up faster than you expect.

common_mistakes.title: Treating tokens the same as words in cost estimates
common_mistakes.explanation: Budgeting by word count is a trap. In English, 1 word is about 1.3 tokens. In code or other languages it can be 2–4× more. Always run `tiktoken` on your actual content to get the real number.

common_mistakes.title: Forgetting that the context limit counts input plus output together
common_mistakes.explanation: A 128k context window counts both the input you send AND the output the model writes. If your prompt uses 120k tokens, you have only 8k left for the reply. The model will cut off or return an error.

recall_questions.q: Explain what a token is, as if to a classmate who has never heard the word.
recall_questions.answer: A token is a small chunk of text — like a word, a syllable, or a punctuation mark — that the AI model reads as one unit. The model never reads whole sentences at once; it reads tokens one by one.

recall_questions.q: Why do LLMs use sub-word tokenization instead of whole words?
recall_questions.answer: Sub-word BPE gives a fixed, manageable vocabulary that handles rare words, new terms, and multiple languages. A whole-word list would need millions of entries and still miss unknown words.

recall_questions.q: Which library lets you count tokens on your computer before calling the OpenAI API?
recall_questions.answer: `tiktoken` — it mirrors OpenAI's exact tokenizer and runs locally with no API cost.

recall_questions.q: What happens if you switch a chatbot from English to Thai, but keep the same token budget?
recall_questions.answer: Thai text uses more tokens per word than English, so the same amount of content will use more tokens. You may hit the context limit sooner and pay more per message.

oa_questions.question: A team estimates their RAG prompt will be '3,000 words' and is surprised when the API throws a context-length error. What are two likely causes?
oa_questions.answer: Word count is not token count — 3,000 words is about 4,000 tokens, not 3,000. Also, the context limit counts input and output tokens together; if the output budget is also being used, the real input limit is smaller. Fix: count with `tiktoken`, not words.
oa_questions.approach: Convert words to tokens (roughly 1.3×) and flag that the context limit is input + output combined. These two points explain almost every 'why did I hit the limit?' surprise.

oa_questions.question: You're building a support bot that handles English and Thai. Your English content costs $0.50 per 1M tokens. A colleague expects Thai to cost the same. Why might it cost significantly more?
oa_questions.answer: Non-Latin scripts often tokenize less efficiently — a Thai word may use 2–3 tokens where an English word uses 1–1.3. The same content in Thai can cost 2–3× more in tokens. Always measure actual token counts for each language on your real content before budgeting.
oa_questions.approach: Anchor on the sub-word vocabulary point: BPE was trained mainly on English, so non-English scripts split into more, smaller pieces.
